faqs.answer: Yes. It is a public beach with free access and public parking. Some hotels front sections of the coast, but the beach itself is open to everyone.

faqs.question: Is the swimming safe?
faqs.answer: The lagoon is shallow, calm and protected by a reef offshore, which makes for easy swimming. However, there are no lifeguards along most of the beach, so children must be supervised and nobody should swim beyond the reef line.

faqs.question: Can you snorkel directly from the beach?
faqs.answer: Yes. Towards the northern end of the public beach, coral patches lie within a short swim of the shore and attract plenty of reef fish. Calm mornings give the best visibility. Please do not touch or stand on the coral.

faqs.question: Is it really the best place for sunset?
faqs.answer: It is among the most reliable. The beach faces west across an open lagoon with nothing blocking the horizon, so the sunset is visible from almost anywhere along the sand. Timing shifts through the year, so check locally on the day.

faqs.question: How busy does it get?
faqs.answer: Weekends and public holidays are busy, since this is a popular beach with Mauritians as well as visitors. Weekday mornings are much quieter, and the beach is long enough that walking away from the parking areas usually finds space.

faqs.question: Is there anywhere to eat nearby?
faqs.answer: Yes. Unlike many Mauritian beaches, Flic en Flac has a village directly behind it with restaurants, shops and street food within easy walking distance of the sand.

faqs.question: What about diving?
faqs.answer: Flic en Flac is the main diving base on the island, with a number of well-known sites offshore. Dives are arranged directly with established local operators, who will advise on conditions and certification requirements.

casela-world-of-adventures.pageTitle: Casela Nature Parks Mauritius | Wildlife & Adventure Visitor Guide
casela-world-of-adventures.pageDescription: A visitor guide to Casela Nature Parks in Cascavelle, Mauritius — 350 hectares of wildlife encounters, safari, aviaries and adventure activities on the west coast.
casela-world-of-adventures.heroSubtitle: Three hundred and fifty hectares of west coast hillside, divided between wildlife, safari plains and adventure.

quickInfo.label: Location
quickInfo.value: Cascavelle, Black River District — west coast

discoverParagraphs: Casela occupies roughly 350 hectares of hillside above the west coast at Cascavelle, and it is best understood as several parks sharing one gate. Some visitors come for the animals, some for the adrenaline, and the ticket structure reflects that — what you can do depends on which package you buy.

The park is organised into distinct zones. A bird kingdom with walk-through aviaries, a family area with gentler rides and a petting farm, an African safari section crossed by safari vehicles with rhino and giraffe among the residents, and a predator area where big cats can be viewed.

On the adventure side there is a long summer toboggan run down the hillside, zip lines, quad and buggy trails, and electric off-road vehicles for exploring the safari terrain. The setting helps: the ground rises steeply behind the coast, so a lot of the park has genuine views out over the lagoon.

Casela also offers close animal interactions, including supervised walks with big cats. These are optional extras rather than part of standard entry, and they are worth thinking about carefully — some visitors are enthusiastic about them, others prefer to stick to observing animals from a distance. Either way, they cost extra and usually need booking.

Entry is sold as a range of packages rather than a single ticket, and what each includes — safari, rides, activities, animal encounters — varies. tamarin-bay.pageTitle: Tamarin Bay Mauritius | Dolphins, Surf & Salt Pans Guide
tamarin-bay.pageDescription: A visitor guide to Tamarin Bay on the west coast of Mauritius — early-morning wild dolphin encounters, a legendary surf break, historic salt pans and responsible visitor advice.
tamarin-bay.heroSubtitle: A west coast fishing village where wild dolphins move through the bay at dawn and a famous surf break rolls in behind them.

discoverParagraphs: Tamarin is a working fishing village on the west coast, set where the Tamarin River reaches the sea beneath a wall of mountains. It has a different feel from the resort stretches north and south of it — lower key, more lived-in, and shaped by three things: dolphins, surf and salt.

Wild dolphins move into the sheltered water off this coast in the early morning, which is why dolphin trips leave not long after first light. Both spinner and bottlenose dolphins are seen here. They are wild animals going about their day, and the quality of the experience depends enormously on whether your boat operator behaves responsibly around them.

Tamarin's surf break made the village internationally known among surfers decades ago and it still draws experienced riders, particularly in the southern winter when the swell is largest. It is not a beginner's wave, and the river mouth adds currents of its own.

Behind the village lie the salt pans — around thirty hectares of shallow evaporation beds that have produced salt here for generations, laid out in geometric blocks against the mountains. They are one of the more photogenic industrial landscapes in Mauritius.

Swimming at Tamarin needs more care than at the calm lagoon beaches elsewhere on the west coast. This is a surf beach with an open swell, and the river mouth can carry strong currents, particularly after heavy rain. It is not a comparable proposition to Flic en Flac.
The salt pans are a working operation rather than a visitor attraction, so access varies. They are clearly visible from the road, and harvesting activity is seasonal.

conservationText: The dolphins off Tamarin are wild animals in their own habitat. They are not fed, trained or contained, and every encounter depends on them choosing to stay nearby.

Boats that crowd, chase or cut across a pod cause real disturbance, particularly to mothers with calves. A responsible operator approaches slowly, keeps a distance, limits time with any one group and never drives into the middle of a pod. If you are choosing a trip, ask how the crew behaves around the animals — it matters more than the price.
Do not touch, chase or attempt to ride dolphins, and follow your skipper's instructions if you enter the water. A calm, patient boat generally sees far more than an aggressive one.

faqs.question: Will I definitely see dolphins at Tamarin?
faqs.answer: No — and any operator who promises otherwise should be treated with caution. These are wild dolphins in open water, and sightings depend on weather, sea conditions and the animals themselves. That said, this coast is the most reliable place in Mauritius to look for them, particularly in the early morning.

faqs.question: Why do dolphin trips leave so early?
faqs.answer: The dolphins are most consistently found in the sheltered water off this coast shortly after dawn, and the sea is usually calmest then. Trips generally depart soon after sunrise, so an early start is unavoidable.

faqs.question: Can I swim with the dolphins?
faqs.answer: Some operators offer in-water time, subject to conditions and to the dolphins' behaviour on the day. If you do enter the water, follow the skipper's instructions exactly, keep your distance, and never touch, chase or attempt to ride an animal.

faqs.question: Is Tamarin good for swimming?
faqs.answer: It needs more care than the calm lagoon beaches nearby. Tamarin is a surf beach with an open swell, and the river mouth can generate strong currents, especially after rain. For easy family swimming on this coast, Flic en Flac is the better choice.

faqs.question: Can beginners surf at Tamarin?
faqs.answer: The Tamarin break is not a beginners' wave — it is powerful and best left to experienced surfers, with the largest swell arriving in the southern winter months. Local surf schools operate at gentler spots elsewhere on the coast.

caudan-waterfront.pageTitle: Caudan Waterfront Port Louis | Shopping, Dining & Harbour Guide
caudan-waterfront.pageDescription: Visit Le Caudan Waterfront in Port Louis, Mauritius. Shops, restaurants, the Blue Penny Museum, the marina and harbour views — plus private transport with MauTravel.
caudan-waterfront.heroSubtitle: The capital's harbourfront quarter. Shops, restaurants, museums and a working marina, built on the old docks where Port Louis has always met the sea.
discoverParagraphs: Le Caudan Waterfront sits on the edge of Port Louis harbour, a few minutes' walk from the Central Market and the old colonial streets of the capital.
The quarter takes its name from Jean Dominique Michel de Caudan, who arrived from Languedoc in the early 18th century and established a saltpan beside this bay in 1726.

For roughly 150 years the peninsula worked as a dock — quays, warehouses, a powder magazine and the Indian Ocean's first meteorological observatory, with the rhythm of the place set by the sugar trade until the Bulk Sugar Terminal took that traffic away in 1980.

The waterfront that stands here now was the first major development of its kind in Mauritius, and it kept the bones of the old port: the wings are named Barkly Wharf, Le Pavillon and Dias Pier, after a colonial governor, a vanished street and the navigator credited with first charting the Mascarenes.
Today it is where the capital comes to eat, shop and walk by the water — and for most visitors, the easiest and most comfortable place to begin a day in Port Louis.

caudan-waterfront.experienceTitle: Two of the World's Most Famous Stamps
caudan-waterfront.experienceDescription: The Blue Penny Museum, which opened at Caudan in November 2001, holds the 1847 Mauritius Blue Penny and Red Penny — among the rarest stamps in existence. They were bought at auction in 1993 for two million dollars by a consortium of Mauritian companies and brought home after nearly 150 years abroad. Because light damages them, the originals are illuminated only for short periods each hour; the rest of the time you see reproductions. The museum also holds Prosper d'Épinay's original 1881 statue of Paul and Virginie, carved from the novel that made Mauritius famous in Europe.

aapravasi-ghat.pageTitle: Aapravasi Ghat Mauritius | UNESCO World Heritage Site Guide
aapravasi-ghat.pageDescription: Visit Aapravasi Ghat in Port Louis, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the immigration depot through which half a million indentured labourers entered Mauritius. Visitor guide and private transport with MauTravel.
aapravasi-ghat.heroSubtitle: A UNESCO World Heritage Site on the Port Louis waterfront. The immigration depot where half a million indentured labourers first set foot in Mauritius — and where the modern nation begins.
discoverParagraphs: Aapravasi Ghat — the Immigration Depot — stands on the Port Louis harbour front, where ships from India, and later from Africa, China and Madagascar, unloaded their passengers.

Between 1849 and 1923, around half a million indentured labourers passed through this depot. Most went on to the sugar estates of Mauritius; others were sent onward to plantations across the British Empire, from the Caribbean to Fiji.

Mauritius was where the system began. After the abolition of slavery, the British chose this island for what they called the 'Great Experiment' — testing whether contracted labour could replace enslaved labour across the empire. What was decided here reshaped the populations of a dozen colonies.

Only partial remains of three stone buildings survive from the original complex, much of it lost to road building in the mid-20th century. What is left is protected as a national monument, and conservation work aims to return the fragile structures to their 1860s condition.

For Mauritius the site is not a ruin but an origin. Around two thirds of the country's population descends from the people who climbed these steps, and the site carries the name Aapravasi Ghat — Hindi for immigration depot — given to it in 1987.

aapravasi-ghat.experienceTitle: Half a Million Journeys, One Set of Steps
aapravasi-ghat.experienceDescription: Slavery was abolished across the British Empire in the 1830s, and Mauritius became the testing ground for what replaced it. Labourers signed contracts — indentures — binding them to years of estate work in return for passage, wages and rations. Many could not read the terms. The voyage from Calcutta or Madras took weeks; on arrival, immigrants climbed the steps at this depot, were registered, given a number, and sent on to the estates. Between 1849 and 1923 around half a million people made that walk. The system spread from here across the empire, and it is the reason Indian communities today form a substantial part of the population of Mauritius, Trinidad, Guyana, Fiji and South Africa.

pereybere.pageTitle: Pereybere Beach Mauritius | North Coast Visitor Guide
pereybere.pageDescription: Visit Pereybere in northern Mauritius — a sheltered public beach with calm, clear water, close to Grand Baie. Swimming, snorkelling, facilities and private transport with MauTravel.
pereybere.heroSubtitle: A small, sheltered public beach on the north coast. Clear shallow water, shade close to the sand, and shops and restaurants a minute's walk away.
discoverParagraphs: Pereybere is a compact public beach on the northern coast, a few minutes up the road from Grand Baie and on the way to Cap Malheureux.
The bay is small and well sheltered, with rocky outcrops at either end holding the sand in place. The water is shallow a long way out and unusually clear, which is what draws people back.
Unlike the long empty stretches elsewhere on the island, Pereybere is a village beach: the road, the shops and the restaurants sit right behind the sand, so nothing is more than a short walk away.
It gets busy — with Mauritian families at weekends as much as with visitors — and that is much of its character. It is a sociable beach rather than a solitary one.

mont-choisy.pageDescription: Visit Mont Choisy in northwest Mauritius — a long crescent of public beach shaded by filao trees, between Trou aux Biches and Grand Baie. Visitor guide and private transport with MauTravel.
mont-choisy.heroSubtitle: A long crescent of public beach on the northwest coast, backed by filao trees and open to a calm lagoon — one of the biggest and best-loved stretches of sand in the north.
discoverParagraphs: Mont Choisy curves along the northwest coast between Trou aux Biches and Grand Baie, one of the longest continuous public beaches in northern Mauritius.

A belt of filao — casuarina — trees runs the length of the sand, dropping a soft carpet of needles and giving shade that lasts all day. It is the reason people bring picnics here rather than just towels.
The bay is protected by the reef offshore, so the lagoon stays calm and shallow. On still mornings the water is flat enough to see the sand ripples through it.
It is a genuinely local beach. Weekends bring Mauritian families with tables, coolers and cooking, and the atmosphere is closer to a public park than a resort strip.

faqs.question: Where is Mont Choisy?
faqs.answer: On the northwest coast of Mauritius, between Trou aux Biches and Grand Baie.

faqs.question: Is Mont Choisy a public beach?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is a free public beach with open access from the coast road.

faqs.question: Is there shade at Mont Choisy?
faqs.answer: Yes. A belt of filao (casuarina) trees runs the length of the beach and provides shade throughout the day.

faqs.question: Is the swimming safe?
faqs.answer: The lagoon is reef-protected, calm and shallow, which makes it popular with families. There are no lifeguards, so supervise children and stay within the lagoon.

faqs.question: How busy does it get?
faqs.answer: Very busy on Sundays and public holidays with Mauritian families. Weekday mornings are much quieter, and the far ends of the beach thin out at any time.

faqs.question: Are there water sports?
faqs.answer: Yes. Independent operators along this stretch of coast run boat trips, glass-bottom boats, parasailing and a submarine excursion.

faqs.question: Is Mont Choisy good for sunset?
faqs.answer: Yes. The bay faces west and is open to the horizon, making it one of the more reliable sunset spots in the north.

trou-aux-biches.pageTitle: Trou aux Biches Mauritius | Beach, Lagoon & Visitor Guide
trou-aux-biches.pageDescription: Visit Trou aux Biches in northern Mauritius — two kilometres of white sand, a calm reef-protected lagoon and some of the island's best snorkelling. Visitor guide and private transport with MauTravel.
trou-aux-biches.heroSubtitle: Two kilometres of white sand under casuarina trees, with a calm lagoon and snorkelling reefs offshore. A former fishing village that became one of the island's best-known beaches — and stayed low-key.
discoverParagraphs: Trou aux Biches sits on the north coast in the district of Pamplemousses, its name already marked on the Lislet-Geoffroy map drawn in 1807, when it was a fishing village under French rule.
The beach runs for around two kilometres — white sand shaded by casuarina trees, with a reef-protected lagoon that stays shallow and calm well out from the shore.

Mauritius' first major hotel was built here in 1971, a few years after independence, and the area has drawn visitors ever since. In 2011 the World Travel Awards named it the World's Leading Beach Destination.

Despite that, it never turned into a resort strip. Trou aux Biches has kept its village shape — a supermarket, boutiques, a few restaurants along the road — and remains noticeably quieter than Grand Baie a short drive north.

trou-aux-biches.experienceTitle: Why the Water Here Is So Calm
trou-aux-biches.experienceDescription: A coral reef runs parallel to this coast a few hundred metres offshore, visible as a line of white water where the ocean swell breaks against it. Everything between that line and the beach is lagoon: shallow, sheltered and largely free of current. It is what makes Trou aux Biches so easy to swim and snorkel at, and why boats can moor here safely. The same reef supports the marine life you come to see — reef fish in the shallows, coral heads within swimming distance of the sand, and dive sites a short boat ride beyond the break.

faqs.question: Where is Trou aux Biches?
faqs.answer: On the north coast of Mauritius, in the district of Pamplemousses, between Mont Choisy and Pointe aux Piments.

faqs.question: How long is the beach?
faqs.answer: Around two kilometres of white sand, shaded along its length by casuarina trees.

faqs.question: Is Trou aux Biches good for snorkelling?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is one of the best beaches in Mauritius for snorkelling straight from the sand, with coral and reef fish within swimming distance of the shore.

faqs.question: Is the swimming safe?
faqs.answer: The lagoon is reef-protected, shallow and calm. There are no lifeguards, so stay within the lagoon, avoid boat channels and supervise children.

faqs.question: Is it busier than Grand Baie?
faqs.answer: No. Trou aux Biches is noticeably quieter and less developed than Grand Baie, while still having shops, a supermarket and restaurants nearby.

faqs.question: What is Trou aux Biches known for?
faqs.answer: Its lagoon, its snorkelling and its sunsets. In 2011 the World Travel Awards named it the World's Leading Beach Destination.

faqs.question: Is there a history to the village?
faqs.answer: Yes. It began as a fishing village and appears on the Lislet-Geoffroy map of 1807. Mauritius' first major hotel was built here in 1971.
